The Moore bound suggests that a 3-regular graph on 14 vertices can't achieve girth 7, so I need to explore other constructions or relax the regularity constraint.

There are 7 antipodal pairs at distance 7 and 14 pairs at distance 6, giving me plenty of options to reach 18 edges while maintaining girth ≥ 7. I'm realizing that adding chords (0,7) and (2,9) creates a problematic 6-cycle, so I need to be more strategic about which chords to include. I'm checking whether chords (0,7) and (6,13) work together—the endpoint 13 is adjacent to 0 on the cycle, which creates a problematic 4-cycle. So I need antipodal chords where all four endpoints are sufficiently spread out on the cycle, at least distance 3 from each other. Testing (0,7) and (3,10) works, but adding a third chord like (6,13) fails because it's too close to the existing endpoints, so I need to find positions that maintain distance ≥ 3 from all four existing endpoints.

Checking the forbidden positions: every vertex on the cycle falls within distance 2 of at least one endpoint from the first two chords, so there's no room for a third antipodal chord. I should try mixing different chord types instead—combining antipodal chords with distance-6 chords, or exploring sparser structures like a 14-cycle with a matching, or checking whether specific chord pairs like (0,6) and (7,13) create acceptable cycle lengths. I'm trying a different approach with two separate 7-cycles connected by cross edges. Adding (0,7) creates a bridge with no short cycles, but (1,9) immediately forms a length-5 cycle, which violates the girth constraint. When I add (2,10) instead, the shortest cycles are length 7 or longer, which works. Now I need to carefully add a third edge while keeping all cycles at least length 7. I'm testing different combinations of three cross edges to satisfy the pairwise cycle length constraints. Most attempts fail because at least one pair violates the minimum distance requirement, but I'm narrowing in on configurations where vertices on the bottom cycle are equidistant from multiple top vertices, which might allow all three pairs to work simultaneously.

Since a single 7-cycle on top is too restrictive, I'm considering whether using longer cycles or a different graph structure altogether—like a tree with carefully placed edges or something inspired by known high-girth graphs like the McGee graph—might give me more flexibility to construct a valid (3,7)-Moore graph.

For this to work, the top vertices involved in cross edges must be spread far apart on their cycle—specifically, pairwise distance at least 2—so that when paired with bottom vertices, the distance constraint can be satisfied.
